## 4. Labellings, pushforwards, and the two structural theorems

### 4.1 Setup

Let $\alpha, \beta, \alpha'$ be finite types. A *labelling* is a map $f : \alpha \to \alpha'$; its *fiber* over $u \in \alpha'$ is $f^{-1}(u) \subseteq \alpha$. For a weight $p$ on $\alpha$ the *pushforward* is
$$(f_* p)(u) \;=\; \sum_{x \in f^{-1}(u)} p(x),$$
and for a joint weight $p$ on $\alpha \times \beta$ we relabel only the first coordinate:
$$(f_\sharp p)(u, y) \;=\; \sum_{x \in f^{-1}(u)} p(x,y).$$
The marginals are $p_1(x) = \sum_y p(x,y)$ and $p_2(y) = \sum_x p(x,y)$, and the *mutual information* in bits is
$$I(p) \;=\; H(p_1) + H(p_2) - H(p).$$

Two elementary identities will be used repeatedly:
$$(f_\sharp p)_1 = f_*(p_1), \qquad (f_\sharp p)_2 = p_2 . \tag{4.1}$$
The first is a reordering of a double sum; the second says that relabelling the first coordinate does not touch the second marginal.

### 4.2 The exact entropy loss of a labelling

**Theorem 4.1 (Loss $=$ total fiber deficit).** For any labelling $f$ and any weight $p$ on $\alpha$,
$$H(p) - H(f_* p) \;=\; \sum_{u \in \alpha'} D_{f^{-1}(u)}(p).$$

*Proof.* The fibers partition $\alpha$, so $H(p) = \sum_u H_{f^{-1}(u)}(p)$. By definition $H(f_*p) = \sum_u \eta\bigl(\sum_{x \in f^{-1}(u)} p(x)\bigr)$. Subtract termwise and apply Definition 3.1. $\square$

**Corollary 4.2 (Labelling cannot create entropy).** If $p \ge 0$ then $H(f_*p) \le H(p)$, by Theorem 3.3.

**Corollary 4.3 (Injective labellings are lossless).** If $f$ is injective, every fiber has at most one element and hence zero deficit, so $H(f_*p) = H(p)$ for every $p$.

The joint version of Theorem 4.1, obtained by slicing over $y \in \beta$, reads
$$H(p) - H(f_\sharp p) \;=\; \sum_{u \in \alpha'}\ \sum_{y \in \beta} D_{f^{-1}(u)}\bigl(p(\cdot, y)\bigr). \tag{4.2}$$

### 4.3 Encoding invariance

**Theorem 4.4 (Encoding invariance).** If $f : \alpha \to \alpha'$ is injective, then for every joint weight $p$ on $\alpha\times\beta$,
$$I(f_\sharp p) \;=\; I(p).$$

*Proof.* By (4.1) and Corollary 4.3, $H\bigl((f_\sharp p)_1\bigr) = H(f_* p_1) = H(p_1)$ and $H\bigl((f_\sharp p)_2\bigr) = H(p_2)$. By (4.2) with all fiber deficits zero, $H(f_\sharp p) = H(p)$. Substituting into the definition of $I$ gives the claim. $\square$

*Interpretation.* A width-valid chained encoding is injective (Corollary 2.4), so mutual information is *notation-independent*: two clean implementations that both satisfy the width criterion are evaluating the same functional of the same data and must agree bit-for-bit. Exact agreement between two independent width-valid pipelines is therefore evidence of correctness, and *approximate* agreement between two allegedly-exact pipelines is itself an anomaly.

### 4.4 The signed data-processing inequality

**Theorem 4.5 (Data-processing for label coarsenings).** For any labelling $f$ (injective or not) and any nonnegative joint weight $p$,
$$I(f_\sharp p) \;\le\; I(p).$$

*Proof.* By (4.1) the second marginal is untouched, so $H\bigl((f_\sharp p)_2\bigr) = H(p_2)$ cancels and
$$I(p) - I(f_\sharp p) \;=\; \underbrace{\bigl[H(p_1) - H(f_* p_1)\bigr]}_{\text{marginal loss}} \;-\; \underbrace{\bigl[H(p) - H(f_\sharp p)\bigr]}_{\text{joint loss}} . \tag{4.3}$$
By Theorem 4.1 the marginal loss equals $\sum_u D_{f^{-1}(u)}(p_1)$, and by (4.2) the joint loss equals $\sum_u \sum_y D_{f^{-1}(u)}\bigl(p(\cdot,y)\bigr)$. Since $p_1 = \sum_{y} p(\cdot,y)$ pointwise, superadditivity of the deficit (Theorem 3.7), applied on each fiber to the family indexed by $y \in \beta$, gives
$$\sum_{y\in\beta} D_{f^{-1}(u)}\bigl(p(\cdot,y)\bigr) \;\le\; D_{f^{-1}(u)}(p_1) \qquad (u \in \alpha').$$
Summing over $u$ shows joint loss $\le$ marginal loss, so the right-hand side of (4.3) is nonnegative. $\square$

**Theorem 4.6 (The reconciliation).** Let $p \ge 0$ be a joint weight on $\alpha \times \beta$, let $f$ be injective (width-valid) and let $g$ be arbitrary. Then
$$I(g_\sharp p) \;\le\; I(f_\sharp p).$$

*Proof.* $I(f_\sharp p) = I(p)$ by Theorem 4.4, and $I(g_\sharp p) \le I(p)$ by Theorem 4.5. $\square$

**Corollary 4.7 (Verdict rule).** If two analyses of the *same* population differ only in their label encoding, and one of the encodings is width-valid, then the larger reported mutual information is the admissible one and the smaller is an artifact. Collision artifacts are *signed*: they can only deflate a measurement, never inflate it.

Applied to §1.1: the width-valid reading of $2.1314$ bits stands; the narrow-frame rebuild's smaller reading is the artifact.

### 4.5 Strictness on the audited population

Domination is an inequality; on the audited population it can be made strict with an explicit margin, using no data beyond the encoding.

**Theorem 4.8 (Strict loss on $P_{4,9}$).** Equip the $36$ pairs of $P_{4,9}$ with the uniform weight $1/36$. Then the width-valid chaining preserves the full label entropy,
$$H\bigl(\text{wide labels}\bigr) \;=\; \log_2 36 \;\approx\; 5.1699\ \text{bits},$$
while the narrow $\cdot 3$ chaining satisfies
$$H\bigl(\text{narrow labels}\bigr) \;\le\; \log_2 36 - \tfrac{1}{18} .$$
In particular the narrow reading is strictly below the wide one.

*Proof.* The wide statement is Corollary 4.3. For the narrow one, the pairs $(0,3)$ and $(1,0)$ both receive label $3$ under $\pi_3$ (Theorem 2.5 with $M=3 < 9 = B$). That fiber therefore contains two atoms of mass $1/36$ each; by Lemma 3.2 its deficit is at least $2 \cdot \tfrac{1}{36}\log_2\frac{2/36}{1/36} = \tfrac{1}{18}$ bit. By Theorem 4.1 the total loss is at least the loss of that single fiber. $\square$

---

## 5. The collapse ceiling: an error bar for the artifact

Theorem 4.6 fixes the *direction* of the discrepancy but not its *size*. Without an upper bound, "collisions did it" is unfalsifiable. This section supplies the missing side.

**Theorem 5.1 (Entropy collapse ceiling).** Let $p$ be a probability weight on $\alpha$ ($p \ge 0$, $\sum_x p(x) = 1$) and let $f$ be a labelling all of whose fibers have at most $k \ge 1$ elements. Then
$$H(p) - H(f_*p) \;\le\; \log_2 k .$$

*Proof.* By Theorem 4.1 the loss is $\sum_u D_{f^{-1}(u)}(p)$. By Theorem 3.8 each term is at most $m_u \log_2 |f^{-1}(u)| \le m_u \log_2 k$, where $m_u = \sum_{x \in f^{-1}(u)} p(x)$ is the mass of the fiber. Since labelling preserves total mass, $\sum_u m_u = 1$, and the bound follows. $\square$

**Theorem 5.2 (Information lost $\le$ label entropy lost).** For any labelling $f$ and any nonnegative joint weight $p$,
$$I(p) - I(f_\sharp p) \;\le\; H(p_1) - H(f_* p_1).$$

*Proof.* From the identity displayed in the proof of Theorem 4.5,
$$I(p) - I(f_\sharp p) = \bigl[H(p_1) - H(f_*p_1)\bigr] - \bigl[H(p) - H(f_\sharp p)\bigr],$$
and the joint loss $H(p)-H(f_\sharp p)$ is nonnegative by (4.2) and Theorem 3.3. $\square$

**Theorem 5.3 (Information collapse ceiling).** Let $p$ be a joint *probability* weight on $\alpha\times\beta$ and let every fiber of $f$ have at most $k \ge 1$ elements. Then
$$I(p) - I(f_\sharp p) \;\le\; \log_2 k .$$

*Proof.* Combine Theorem 5.2 with Theorem 5.1 applied to the first marginal $p_1$, which is a probability weight on $\alpha$. $\square$

**Corollary 5.4 (A two-to-one merge costs at most one bit).** If no label collects more than two classes, then $I(p) - I(f_\sharp p) \le 1$, whatever the size of $\alpha$, $\beta$, or the strength of the channel.

**Corollary 5.5 (Audit contrapositive).** If two readings of a probability population differ by more than one bit of mutual information and the difference is attributed to a label merge, then some label must collect at least three distinct classes. Pairwise merging *cannot* account for a drop exceeding one bit.

**Theorem 5.6 (Sandwich).** For a probability weight $p$ and a $k$-bounded labelling,
$$0 \;\le\; H(p) - H(f_*p) \;\le\; \log_2 k,$$
and by Theorem 3.9 the upper end is attained (a uniform $k$-atom fiber carrying all the mass loses exactly $\log_2 k$), so no smaller universal ceiling exists.

### 5.1 The audited population, quantitatively

Under the narrow $\cdot 3$ frame on $P_{4,9}$, direct inspection of the strips shows that no label collects more than three of the $36$ pairs; the maximal fibers are the three-element ones in the overlap region. Hence, by Theorem 5.3:

**Corollary 5.7.** For any probability weight on $P_{4,9}\times\beta$, the narrow-frame relabelling can destroy at most
$$\log_2 3 \;\approx\; 1.5850 \ \text{bits}$$
of mutual information, while the width-valid relabelling destroys exactly zero (Theorem 4.4).

---

## 6. The audit protocol

The theory above compiles into three checks. The first is *preventive* and costs nothing; the last two are *forensic* and can be run on a printed results table with no access to raw data.

**Check W (width).** Before running: for a chained key $\sum_i a_i M_i$ with $M_1 = 1$, verify $M_{i+1} \ge A_i M_i$ for every $i$, where $A_i$ is the alphabet size of dial $i$. By Theorem 2.6 this is *exactly* the no-collision condition — not a sufficient heuristic but an equivalence. If it fails, the predicted label count is $M(A-1)+B$ (Corollary 2.9) in the two-dial case, and the discrepancy against $A\cdot B$ tells you how many classes were merged.

**Check D (direction).** Given two readings of the same population that differ only in encoding, with one encoding width-valid: the width-valid reading dominates (Theorem 4.6). The smaller reading is the artifact. This is a verdict, not a preference.

**Check C (ceiling).** Given the maximal fiber size $k$ of the suspect encoding — computable from the encoding alone — the gap between the two readings must satisfy $\Delta I \le \log_2 k$ (Theorem 5.3), and additionally $\Delta I \le \Delta H$ where $\Delta H$ is the drop in label entropy (Theorem 5.2). A violation of either inequality *proves* that the two pipelines differ in something beyond the label encoding, and the investigation must continue.

### 6.1 Running the protocol on the disputed rows

| construction | frame | distinct labels | $H(\text{labels})$ | $I(\text{joint})$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| original | $a\cdot 10000 + b$ | $36$ | $4.6006$ | $2.1314$ |
| independent clean re-implementation | width-valid | $36$ | $4.6006$ | $2.1314$ |
| rebuild | nested $\cdot 10$ inside $\cdot 100$ | $18$ | $3.6073$ | $0.5830$ |

*Check W.* The rebuild's inner frame is narrower than the combined alphabet below it, so by Theorem 2.6 the encoding certainly collides; by Corollary 2.9 the collapsed class count is a determinate function of $(A,B,M)$, and the observed $36 \to 18$ is exactly the predicted $M(A-1)+B$ with $(A,B,M) = (4,9,3)$.

*Check D.* The original encoding is width-valid; the rebuild's is not; both act on the same population. Theorem 4.6 therefore places the rebuild's reading below the original's, and the original's $2.1314$ bits is the admissible value. The independent clean re-implementation reproduces $2.1314$ *exactly*, which is what Theorem 4.4 predicts for two width-valid encodings — exact agreement, not agreement to within noise.

*Check C.* The maximal fiber under the narrow frame is $3$, so the ceiling on the information drop is $\log_2 3 \approx 1.5850$ bits. The observed drop is $2.1314 - 0.5830 = 1.5484$ bits, which clears the ceiling with $0.0366$ bits of margin: the collision explanation is quantitatively admissible.

The second half of Check C is more informative, and we record it as a flag rather than a confirmation. The observed label-entropy drop is $4.6006 - 3.6073 = 0.9933$ bits, while the observed information drop is $1.5484$ bits. Theorem 5.2 forbids $\Delta I > \Delta H$ for a *single* coarsening of a fixed joint weight. The two rows therefore cannot differ only by one merge of the joint label: at least one further difference — a second compression stage, a different marginalisation, or a different population restriction — is present in the rebuild. This is exactly the intended use of the protocol: the ceiling confirms that collisions can explain the magnitude, while the sharp inequality localises a residual discrepancy that a re-run should target.

For calibration, the reported per-coordinate marginals are $1.0012$ bits each, summing to $2.0024$ against a joint value of $2.1314$; the excess of about $0.129$ bits is genuine synergy between the two dials, which is precisely the quantity that a class merge destroys first.

## 7. Algorithms

**Algorithm 1 (Width audit for a multi-field chained key).** Input: alphabet sizes $A_1,\dots,A_r$ and frames $M_1,\dots,M_r$ with $M_1 = 1$. Output: `VALID`, or the first violating index together with the predicted number of merged classes. Complexity: $O(r)$ integer operations. Correctness: Theorem 2.6 iterated.

**Algorithm 2 (Exact collapse count).** Input: $A$, $B$, $M$. Output: the number of distinct labels, namely $A\cdot B$ if $M \ge B$ and $M(A-1) + B$ otherwise. Complexity: $O(1)$. Correctness: Theorems 2.7 and Corollary 2.9. This is the lookup an experimenter should consult *before* running.

**Algorithm 3 (Fiber profile and collapse ceiling).** Input: $A$, $B$, $M$ with $M \le B$. Output: for each label $n < M(A-1)+B$, the fiber size $|\{a < A : 0 \le n - aM < B\}|$; hence the maximal fiber $k$ and the ceiling $\log_2 k$ on both the entropy and the information that the frame can destroy. Complexity: $O(AB)$ by direct enumeration, or $O(1)$ per label with the closed form $|\{a : \max(0,\lceil (n-B+1)/M\rceil) \le a \le \min(A-1, \lfloor n/M\rfloor)\}|$. Correctness: Theorems 5.1 and 5.3.

**Algorithm 4 (Forensic reconciliation of two readings).** Input: two rows $(\text{labels}, H, I)$ from the same population, plus the encodings. Output: a verdict (which reading is admissible) and a consistency report. Steps: run Algorithm 1 on each encoding; if exactly one is valid, the valid one's $I$ is admissible (Check D); compute $k$ via Algorithm 3 and test $\Delta I \le \log_2 k$ and $\Delta I \le \Delta H$; report any violation as evidence of an undocumented second difference between the pipelines. Complexity: dominated by Algorithm 3.

---

## 8. Discussion

### 8.1 What is genuinely new here

Each ingredient is individually classical — division with remainder, Gibbs' inequality, concavity of entropy, the data-processing inequality. What the present work contributes is their assembly into a *decision procedure for a disputed measurement*, together with three sharpenings that the classical statements do not supply directly:

1. **An exact, not asymptotic, collapse count.** $M(A-1)+B$ is the precise number of surviving classes, with the image identified as an unbroken interval (Theorem 2.8). Most treatments of hash collisions are probabilistic; here the structure is deterministic and fully resolved.
2. **A signed verdict rule.** Theorem 4.6 says a fixed population cannot be over-read by a bad encoding. This turns the usual "two runs disagree" stalemate into an ordering.
3. **A two-sided error bar with attainability.** Theorems 5.1–5.6 bound the damage by $\log_2 k$, and Theorem 3.9 shows the bound is achieved, so the audit test is as tight as any universal test can be.

The deficit calculus of §3 is also of independent use: it is a self-contained treatment of Shannon entropy for *unnormalised* finitely supported weights, which is the natural setting for fiberwise arguments, and it flags the absolute-continuity subtlety (Theorem 3.6) that the $0\log 0 = 0$ convention conceals.

### 8.2 Limitations

* The ceiling $\log_2 k$ uses only the *largest* fiber. The true loss is the mass-weighted average $\sum_u m_u \log_2 |f^{-1}(u)|$, which for a chained frame is an explicit arithmetic object (Algorithm 3). A sharper, profile-dependent ceiling is available and is the first item in §9.
* Theorem 4.6 compares two encodings of a *fixed* population. If two runs also differ in filtering, binning, or estimator, the verdict rule does not apply directly — though Theorem 5.2 will typically detect the difference, as it did in §6.1.
* Everything is stated for finite alphabets and exact (plug-in) entropies. Finite-sample estimation bias is a separate, well-studied source of discrepancy and is not modelled here; notably, plug-in mutual information is biased *upward* on small samples, in the opposite direction to a collision artifact, which makes the two failure modes distinguishable in principle.

### 8.3 Practical recommendations

Use a struct, a tuple, or a factorised index rather than a chained integer wherever the language permits. Where chaining is unavoidable — sparse indices, database keys, GPU kernels — compute frames from measured alphabet sizes rather than from decimal aesthetics ($10$, $100$, $10000$ are chosen for readability, and readability is not a correctness criterion), and assert the mixed-radix condition at pipeline entry. Log the distinct-label count alongside every joint statistic: a discrepancy against the product of the alphabet sizes is a zero-cost detector of exactly this bug.

---

## 9. Future directions

**Sharp collapse ceiling from the fiber profile.** The ceiling $\log_2 k$ uses only the largest fiber, whereas the true loss is the mass-weighted average $\sum_u m_u \log_2 |F_u|$, and for a chained frame the whole fiber profile is an explicit arithmetic object: under $M \le B$ the fiber over $n$ has size $|\{a < A : 0 \le n - Ma < B\}|$. Combining the per-fiber deficit bound with the exact label set yields a *closed formula* for the worst-case entropy loss of an $(A,B,M)$ frame — a lookup table an audit can consult before running an experiment.

**Reconstructibility: when is the true channel recoverable?** The data-processing inequality has a computable defect — the fiber deficits — so a coarsened reading together with the fiber profile bounds the true reading from *both* sides; for a $k$-bounded distortion the true value can be reconstructed from the collapsed one to within $\log_2 k$. Retracted rows currently have to be re-run from scratch; a reconstruction bracket would let a retracted number be repaired rather than discarded, at the cost of a widened error bar.

**Multi-dial chaining and a width calculus.** Chaining $r$ dials as $\sum_i a_i M_i$ is injective precisely under the mixed-radix condition $M_i \ge A_{i-1}M_{i-1}$ (with $M_1 = 1$), so width checking becomes a small calculus on frame vectors, with a canonical minimal-frame normal form and a notion of "slack" measuring how much headroom a key has before a new category breaks it.

**Estimator-level integration.** Combining the collapse ceiling with finite-sample bias bounds for plug-in entropy estimators would give a single interval within which two readings of one population must lie if they differ only by encoding and sampling — a complete forensic bracket.

---

## 10. Conclusion

A chained integer label $\pi_M(a,b) = aM+b$ is faithful if and only if the frame dominates the inner alphabet, $B \le M$; otherwise it collides, on every population with at least two outer codes, and reports exactly $M(A-1)+B$ classes in place of $A\cdot B$. On a $4\times 9$ population with $M=3$ this is $18$ in place of $36$ — half the classes, gone silently.

Merging classes destroys entropy (strictly, whenever two merged classes are populated) and can only *decrease* measured mutual information, while an injective re-encoding changes nothing at all. Hence, on a fixed population, a width-valid reading dominates every other reading: when two analyses disagree and one is width-valid, the larger value is the admissible one. And the damage is bounded: a $k$-bounded merge destroys at most $\log_2 k$ bits of label entropy and at most $\log_2 k$ bits of information, with the bound attained, so "collisions did it" is a falsifiable claim with an explicit error bar.

The lesson generalises beyond one disputed measurement: whenever discrete fields are packed into a single integer key, width-check the frames against the alphabets. The check is $O(1)$, and it is not merely sufficient — it is exactly equivalent to the absence of the bug.

\begin{abstract}
Experimental and statistical pipelines routinely encode a pair of discrete codes $(a,b)$ as a single integer \emph{chained label} $\pi_M(a,b) = aM + b$ for a fixed decimal \emph{frame} $M$. We prove that this encoding is injective on $\{0,\dots,A-1\}\times\{0,\dots,B-1\}$ if and only if $B \le M$, and that when the frame is narrow the failure is structural rather than data-dependent: an explicit collision exists for every population with at least two outer codes. For a narrow frame $M \le B$ we determine the image exactly --- it is the unbroken integer interval $[0,\,M(A-1)+B)$ --- so the number of distinct labels reported is exactly $M(A-1)+B$ against $A\cdot B$ genuine pairs, strictly fewer whenever $M<B$ and $A \ge 2$. Specialising to a $4\times 9$ population and the frame $M=3$ gives the arithmetic signature $36 \mapsto 18$: exactly half the classes are silently merged. We then develop, from first principles, an entropy-deficit calculus for finitely supported nonnegative weights in bits: the deficit of a block is nonnegative, strictly positive when two atoms carry positive mass, bounded by $S\log_2|s|$ with equality for the uniform block, and superadditive under splitting. As a by-product we record a counterexample showing that Gibbs' inequality genuinely fails under the $0\log 0 = 0$ convention if absolute continuity is dropped. From this calculus we obtain two structural theorems: \emph{encoding invariance} (an injective relabelling of one coordinate leaves mutual information unchanged) and a \emph{signed data-processing inequality} (an arbitrary relabelling can only decrease it). Consequently, on a fixed population a width-valid reading dominates every other reading, so a disagreement can be resolved only in its favour. Finally we give a \emph{collapse ceiling}: if no label collects more than $k$ classes, at most $\log_2 k$ bits of label entropy and at most $\log_2 k$ bits of mutual information can be destroyed; a two-to-one merge costs at most one bit; a drop exceeding one bit proves the existence of a label collecting at least three classes; and the information destroyed never exceeds the label entropy destroyed. These bounds turn the informal lesson ``width-check chained encodings'' into a falsifiable audit protocol with a two-sided error bar, executable on a printed results table.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} chained integer encoding, mixed radix, label collision, Shannon entropy, entropy deficit, Gibbs' inequality, data-processing inequality, mutual information, reproducibility audit.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The disputed measurement}

A joint-channel measurement on a fixed population of paired discrete codes was reported twice. The original analysis reported $36$ distinct joint labels, a label entropy of $4.6006$ bits, and a mutual information of $2.1314$ bits, with per-coordinate marginals of $1.0012$ bits each. A later rebuild of the same analysis on the same population reported $18$ distinct joint labels, a label entropy of $3.6073$ bits, and a mutual information of $0.5830$ bits.

The two constructions differed in exactly one documented respect: the arithmetic frame used to chain the two component codes into a single integer. The original used $\pi(a,b) = a\cdot 10000 + b$; the rebuild used a $\cdot 10$ frame for the inner code nested inside a $\cdot 100$ frame for a six-valued outer code.

The question answered here is not which run to trust --- a sociological question --- but the mathematical one underneath: \emph{given only the encodings, and no access to either run's data, is one of the two readings necessarily wrong, and in which direction?} The answer is yes, and it decomposes into arithmetic (\S\ref{sec:arith}), an entropy calculus (\S\ref{sec:deficit}), and adjudication (\S\ref{sec:struct}--\S\ref{sec:ceiling}).

\subsection{Why this is not merely a bug report}

Chaining is ubiquitous: contingency-table strata, group-by keys, sparse index arithmetic, feature hashing, and every ad-hoc ``combine two categorical variables'' idiom. The failure mode is \emph{silent} (no exception is raised; a well-defined statistic of a coarsened population is returned), \emph{deterministic and reproducible} (re-running the code reproduces the wrong number exactly, so reproducibility checks miss it), and \emph{conservative-looking} (by Theorem~\ref{thm:dpi}, merging can only lower measured information, so the corrupted reading resembles a cautious reanalysis). The last property is why a \emph{signed} theorem is worth having: knowing the direction of the bias converts a stalemate into a verdict.

\section{The arithmetic of chained labels}\label{sec:arith}

\begin{definition}[Chained label]
For a frame $M \in \NN$ and codes $a,b \in \NN$, the \emph{chained label} is $\pi_M(a,b) = aM+b$. We call $a$ the \emph{outer code}, $b$ the \emph{inner code}, and $M$ the \emph{frame}. The \emph{code population} with alphabet sizes $A,B$ is $P_{A,B} = \{0,\dots,A-1\}\times\{0,\dots,B-1\}$, of cardinality $A\cdot B$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Width validity]
The frame $M$ is \emph{width-valid} for an inner alphabet of size $B$ if $B \le M$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Width criterion, sufficiency]\label{thm:inj}
If $b < M$, $b' < M$ and $aM+b = a'M+b'$, then $a=a'$ and $b=b'$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
From $b<M$ we get $M>0$. Division with remainder is the decoder: $\lfloor (aM+b)/M\rfloor = a$ since $\lfloor b/M \rfloor = 0$, and likewise for $a'$. Hence $a = a'$ from equality of the labels, and $b=b'$ by cancellation.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:injpop}
If $B \le M$ then $(a,b)\mapsto \pi_M(a,b)$ is injective on $P_{A,B}$ for every $A$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Narrow frames always collide]\label{thm:collide}
Let $M < B$ and $A \ge 2$. Then $(0,M) \neq (1,0)$ are both in $P_{A,B}$ and
\[
\pi_M(0,M) \;=\; M \;=\; \pi_M(1,0).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Admissibility: $M<B$ makes $(0,M)$ legal, $A\ge2$ makes $(1,0)$ legal. Evaluating $\pi_M$ gives $M$ in both cases.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Width validity $=$ no collisions]\label{thm:iff}
Fix $A\ge 2$ and $B$. Then $B \le M$ if and only if for all $(a,b),(a',b') \in P_{A,B}$, $\pi_M(a,b)=\pi_M(a',b')$ implies $(a,b)=(a',b')$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Forward: Theorem~\ref{thm:inj}. Backward: contrapositive via Theorem~\ref{thm:collide}.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:iff} says the runtime check \verb|inner_alphabet_size <= frame| is neither conservative nor optimistic: it is \emph{equivalent} to correctness of the encoding.

\begin{theorem}[Wide frame preserves all classes]\label{thm:wide}
If $B \le M$ then $\lvert \pi_M(P_{A,B})\rvert = A\cdot B$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Immediate from Corollary~\ref{cor:injpop}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The narrow image is an interval]\label{thm:interval}
If $M \le B$ and $A \ge 1$ then
\[
\pi_M(P_{A,B}) \;=\; \{0,1,\dots,\,M(A-1)+B-1\}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\subseteq$) For $a \le A-1$, $b<B$: $aM+b \le (A-1)M + b < M(A-1)+B$.

($\supseteq$) Let $n < M(A-1)+B$. If $n < M(A-1)$ then $M>0$, and $a = \lfloor n/M\rfloor$, $b = n \bmod M$ satisfy $a < A-1$, $b < M \le B$ and $aM+b=n$. Otherwise $n \ge M(A-1)$ and we take $a = A-1$, $b = n - M(A-1)$, so $0 \le b < B$ and $aM+b = n$.
\end{proof}

Geometrically, outer value $a$ contributes the strip $[aM,\,aM+B)$; consecutive strips are offset by $M$ but have length $B \ge M$, so they overlap like roof shingles and their union is unbroken.

\begin{corollary}[Exact narrow-frame label count]\label{cor:count}
If $M \le B$ and $A \ge 1$ then $\lvert \pi_M(P_{A,B})\rvert = M(A-1)+B$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Strict loss]\label{thm:strictcount}
If $M<B$ and $A \ge 2$ then $M(A-1)+B < A\cdot B$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Since $M \le B-1$ we have $M(A-1) \le (B-1)(A-1)$, so
$M(A-1)+B \le (B-1)(A-1)+B = AB - (A-1) < AB$ as $A \ge 2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The audited instance]\label{cor:audited}
On $P_{4,9}$ (that is, $36$ pairs): the width-valid frame $M=10000$ reports $36$ labels; the narrow frame $M=3$ reports $3(4-1)+9 = 18$; hence the narrow frame reports exactly half the classes.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}[Multi-field chaining]
The criterion iterates: chaining $r$ dials as $\sum_{i=1}^r a_i M_i$ with $M_1=1$ is injective on $\prod_i\{0,\dots,A_i-1\}$ precisely under the mixed-radix condition $M_{i+1} \ge A_i M_i$, since each nested chaining must be width-valid against the combined alphabet below it.
\end{remark}

\section{An entropy-deficit calculus}\label{sec:deficit}

\begin{definition}
For $t \in \RR$ put $\eta(t) = -t\log_2 t$ with $\eta(0)=0$. For a finite index set $s$ and a weight function $w$, the \emph{entropy in bits} is $H_s(w) = \sum_{i\in s}\eta(w_i)$, and the \emph{deficit}, i.e.\ the entropy destroyed by collapsing $s$ into a single atom, is
\[
D_s(w) \;=\; H_s(w) \;-\; \eta\!\Bigl(\sum_{i\in s} w_i\Bigr).
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Closed form]\label{lem:closed}
With $S = \sum_{j\in s} w_j$,
\[
D_s(w) \;=\; \sum_{i\in s} w_i\bigl(\log_2 S - \log_2 w_i\bigr).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Purely algebraic: $S\log_2 S = \sum_{i\in s} w_i\log_2 S$, and $D_s(w) = -\sum_i w_i\log_2 w_i + \sum_i w_i \log_2 S$. No positivity is used.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Merging destroys entropy]\label{thm:Dnonneg}
If $w_i \ge 0$ for all $i \in s$ then $D_s(w)\ge 0$; equivalently $\eta(\sum_i w_i) \le H_s(w)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Each term of Lemma~\ref{lem:closed} is nonnegative: for $w_i=0$ it vanishes; for $w_i>0$ we have $w_i \le S$, so $\log_2 w_i \le \log_2 S$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Strict loss]\label{thm:Dpos}
If $w \ge 0$ on $s$ and there are distinct $i,j\in s$ with $w_i>0$, $w_j>0$, then $D_s(w)>0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Now $S \ge w_i+w_j > w_i$, so $\log_2 w_i < \log_2 S$ and the $i$-th term is strictly positive; the rest are nonnegative.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Unnormalised Gibbs inequality, base 2]\label{thm:gibbs}
Let $a,b \ge 0$ on a finite $s$ with (i) $b_i = 0 \Rightarrow a_i=0$ and (ii) $\sum_i b_i \le \sum_i a_i$. Then $\sum_{i\in s} a_i(\log_2 a_i - \log_2 b_i) \ge 0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Per term, from $\log x \le x-1$: for $a_i>0$ (so $b_i>0$ by (i)), $\log(b_i/a_i)\le b_i/a_i-1$ gives $a_i(\log a_i - \log b_i)\ge a_i-b_i$; divide by $\log 2>0$. For $a_i=0$ the left side is $0 \ge -b_i/\log 2$. Summing telescopes the right side to $(\sum a_i - \sum b_i)/\log 2 \ge 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Absolute continuity is necessary]\label{thm:gibbsctr}
Under the convention $\log_2 0 = 0$, hypothesis (i) of Theorem~\ref{thm:gibbs} cannot be dropped: with $s=\{0,1\}$, $a=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$, $b=(1,0)$ one has $\sum b = \sum a = 1$ but
\[
\sum_i a_i(\log_2 a_i - \log_2 b_i) = \tfrac12(-1-0)+\tfrac12(-1-0) = -1 < 0 .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Superadditivity of the deficit]\label{thm:super}
Let $\{v^{(y)}\}_{y\in t}$ be a finite family of nonnegative weights on $s$ and $w = \sum_{y} v^{(y)}$ pointwise. Then $\sum_{y\in t} D_s(v^{(y)}) \le D_s(w)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
If the total mass $W = \sum_{x} w_x$ vanishes, all weights vanish and both sides are $0$. Otherwise put $V_y = \sum_x v^{(y)}_x$ and compare $v^{(y)}$ against the tilted measure $b^{(y)}_x = w_x V_y / W$, which has the same total mass $V_y$ and satisfies the absolute-continuity hypothesis. Theorem~\ref{thm:gibbs} gives $0 \le \sum_x v^{(y)}_x(\log_2 v^{(y)}_x - \log_2 b^{(y)}_x)$, and expanding $\log_2 b^{(y)}_x = \log_2 w_x + \log_2 V_y - \log_2 W$ rewrites the right-hand side as
\[
\sum_x v^{(y)}_x\Bigl[\bigl(\log_2 W - \log_2 w_x\bigr) - \bigl(\log_2 V_y - \log_2 v^{(y)}_x\bigr)\Bigr].
\]
Summing over $y$ and using $\sum_y v^{(y)}_x = w_x$, the first bracket sums to $D_s(w)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:closed} and the second to $\sum_y D_s(v^{(y)})$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Deficit ceiling]\label{thm:blockceil}
For nonnegative $w$ on a finite block $s$ with total mass $S$, $D_s(w) \le S\log_2\lvert s\rvert$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
For $S=0$ both sides vanish. For $S>0$ compare $w$ with the uniform weight $u_i = S/\lvert s\rvert$ of the same total mass; Theorem~\ref{thm:gibbs} gives $\sum_i w_i(\log_2 w_i - \log_2 u_i)\ge 0$, which rearranges into the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The ceiling is attained]\label{thm:attain}
For nonempty $s$ and $w_i = 1/\lvert s\rvert$, $D_s(w) = \log_2\lvert s\rvert$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$S=1$, so each term of Lemma~\ref{lem:closed} equals $\tfrac{1}{\lvert s\rvert}\log_2\lvert s\rvert$, and there are $\lvert s\rvert$ terms.
\end{proof}

\section{Labellings and the two structural theorems}\label{sec:struct}

Let $\alpha,\beta,\alpha'$ be finite. A \emph{labelling} is $f:\alpha\to\alpha'$ with fibers $f^{-1}(u)$. For a weight $p$ on $\alpha$, the pushforward is $(f_*p)(u) = \sum_{x\in f^{-1}(u)} p(x)$; for a joint weight $p$ on $\alpha\times\beta$ we relabel the first coordinate,
\[
(f_\sharp p)(u,y) \;=\; \sum_{x \in f^{-1}(u)} p(x,y).
\]
The marginals are $p_1(x) = \sum_y p(x,y)$, $p_2(y) = \sum_x p(x,y)$, and the mutual information in bits is $I(p) = H(p_1)+H(p_2)-H(p)$. Two identities are used repeatedly:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marg}
(f_\sharp p)_1 = f_*(p_1), \qquad (f_\sharp p)_2 = p_2 .
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Loss equals total fiber deficit]\label{thm:lossfiber}
For any labelling $f$ and weight $p$ on $\alpha$,
\[
H(p) - H(f_*p) \;=\; \sum_{u\in\alpha'} D_{f^{-1}(u)}(p).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The fibers partition $\alpha$, so $H(p) = \sum_u H_{f^{-1}(u)}(p)$, while $H(f_*p) = \sum_u \eta\bigl(\sum_{x\in f^{-1}(u)}p(x)\bigr)$. Subtract termwise.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:nocreate}
If $p \ge 0$ then $H(f_*p) \le H(p)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:Dnonneg}). If $f$ is injective, every fiber is a singleton, so $H(f_*p) = H(p)$ for all $p$.
\end{corollary}

Slicing Theorem~\ref{thm:lossfiber} over $y\in\beta$ gives the joint version
\begin{equation}\label{eq:jointloss}
H(p) - H(f_\sharp p) \;=\; \sum_{u\in\alpha'}\sum_{y\in\beta} D_{f^{-1}(u)}\bigl(p(\cdot,y)\bigr).
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Encoding invariance]\label{thm:inv}
If $f$ is injective then $I(f_\sharp p) = I(p)$ for every joint weight $p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By \eqref{eq:marg} and Corollary~\ref{cor:nocreate}, $H((f_\sharp p)_1) = H(f_*p_1) = H(p_1)$ and $H((f_\sharp p)_2) = H(p_2)$. By \eqref{eq:jointloss} with all fiber deficits zero, $H(f_\sharp p) = H(p)$. Substitute into the definition of $I$.
\end{proof}

A width-valid chained encoding is injective (Corollary~\ref{cor:injpop}), so mutual information is notation-independent: two clean implementations that both satisfy the width criterion must agree bit-for-bit, and merely \emph{approximate} agreement between two allegedly exact pipelines is itself an anomaly.

\begin{theorem}[Data-processing for label coarsenings]\label{thm:dpi}
For any labelling $f$ and nonnegative joint weight $p$, $I(f_\sharp p) \le I(p)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By \eqref{eq:marg} the second marginal cancels, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:split}
I(p) - I(f_\sharp p) \;=\; \bigl[H(p_1) - H(f_*p_1)\bigr] \;-\; \bigl[H(p)-H(f_\sharp p)\bigr].
\end{equation}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:lossfiber} the first bracket is $\sum_u D_{f^{-1}(u)}(p_1)$; by \eqref{eq:jointloss} the second is $\sum_u\sum_y D_{f^{-1}(u)}(p(\cdot,y))$. Since $p_1 = \sum_y p(\cdot,y)$, Theorem~\ref{thm:super} applied on each fiber gives $\sum_y D_{f^{-1}(u)}(p(\cdot,y)) \le D_{f^{-1}(u)}(p_1)$; summing over $u$ makes \eqref{eq:split} nonnegative.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The reconciliation]\label{thm:recon}
Let $p\ge0$ be a joint weight, $f$ injective (width-valid) and $g$ arbitrary. Then $I(g_\sharp p) \le I(f_\sharp p)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$I(f_\sharp p) = I(p)$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:inv}, and $I(g_\sharp p)\le I(p)$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:dpi}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Verdict rule]
If two analyses of the same population differ only in their label encoding and one encoding is width-valid, the larger reported mutual information is the admissible one and the smaller is an artifact. Collision artifacts are \emph{signed}: they deflate, never inflate.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Strict loss on the audited population]\label{thm:strict49}
Equip the $36$ pairs of $P_{4,9}$ with the uniform weight $1/36$. The width-valid chaining preserves the full label entropy $\log_2 36 \approx 5.1699$ bits, while the narrow $\cdot 3$ chaining satisfies
\[
H(\text{narrow labels}) \;\le\; \log_2 36 - \tfrac{1}{18}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The wide case is Corollary~\ref{cor:nocreate}. For the narrow case, $(0,3)$ and $(1,0)$ share the label $3$ under $\pi_3$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:collide} with $M=3<9=B$), so that fiber holds two atoms of mass $1/36$ and, by Lemma~\ref{lem:closed}, has deficit at least $2\cdot\tfrac{1}{36}\log_2 2 = \tfrac{1}{18}$. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:lossfiber}.
\end{proof}

\section{The collapse ceiling}\label{sec:ceiling}

\begin{theorem}[Entropy collapse ceiling]\label{thm:Hceil}
Let $p$ be a probability weight on $\alpha$ and let every fiber of $f$ have at most $k \ge 1$ elements. Then $H(p) - H(f_*p) \le \log_2 k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:lossfiber} the loss is $\sum_u D_{f^{-1}(u)}(p)$, and by Theorem~\ref{thm:blockceil} each term is at most $m_u\log_2 k$ with $m_u$ the fiber mass. Labelling preserves mass, so $\sum_u m_u = 1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Information lost never exceeds label entropy lost]\label{thm:MIleH}
For any labelling $f$ and nonnegative joint weight $p$,
\[
I(p) - I(f_\sharp p) \;\le\; H(p_1) - H(f_*p_1).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By \eqref{eq:split} the difference of the two sides is the joint loss $H(p)-H(f_\sharp p)$, which is nonnegative by \eqref{eq:jointloss} and Theorem~\ref{thm:Dnonneg}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Information collapse ceiling]\label{thm:MIceil}
Let $p$ be a joint probability weight and let every fiber of $f$ have at most $k\ge1$ elements. Then $I(p)-I(f_\sharp p) \le \log_2 k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Combine Theorem~\ref{thm:MIleH} with Theorem~\ref{thm:Hceil} applied to $p_1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A two-to-one merge costs at most one bit]\label{cor:onebit}
If no label collects more than two classes then $I(p)-I(f_\sharp p) \le 1$, whatever the size of $\alpha$, $\beta$ or the strength of the channel.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[Audit contrapositive]
If two readings of a probability population differ by more than one bit and the difference is attributed to a label merge, some label must collect at least three distinct classes.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Sandwich, and sharpness]
For a probability weight and a $k$-bounded labelling, $0 \le H(p)-H(f_*p)\le \log_2 k$, and by Theorem~\ref{thm:attain} the upper end is attained; no smaller universal ceiling exists.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}[The audited population, quantitatively]\label{cor:auditceil}
Under the narrow $\cdot 3$ frame on $P_{4,9}$ no label collects more than three pairs, so the frame destroys at most $\log_2 3 \approx 1.5850$ bits of mutual information, while a width-valid frame destroys exactly zero.
\end{corollary}

\section{The audit protocol}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Check W --- width]
Before running: for a chained key $\sum_i a_i M_i$ with $M_1=1$, verify $M_{i+1}\ge A_iM_i$ for all $i$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:iff} this is exactly the no-collision condition. If it fails, the predicted two-dial label count is $M(A-1)+B$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:count}).
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Check D --- direction]
Given two readings of one population differing only in encoding, with one encoding width-valid: the width-valid reading dominates (Theorem~\ref{thm:recon}); the smaller reading is the artifact.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Check C --- ceiling]
With $k$ the maximal fiber size of the suspect encoding, the gap must satisfy $\Delta I \le \log_2 k$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:MIceil}) and $\Delta I \le \Delta H$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:MIleH}). A violation proves the pipelines differ in more than the encoding.
\end{algorithmbox}

\emph{Check W.} The rebuild's inner frame is narrower than the combined alphabet below it, so by Theorem~\ref{thm:iff} the encoding certainly collides, and the observed $36\to18$ is exactly $M(A-1)+B$ with $(A,B,M)=(4,9,3)$.

\emph{Check D.} The original encoding is width-valid, the rebuild's is not, and both act on the same population; Theorem~\ref{thm:recon} places the rebuild below the original, so $2.1314$ bits is the admissible value. The independent clean re-implementation reproduces it \emph{exactly}, as Theorem~\ref{thm:inv} predicts for two width-valid encodings.

\emph{Check C.} The maximal narrow-frame fiber is $3$, so the ceiling is $\log_2 3 \approx 1.5850$ bits; the observed drop $2.1314-0.5830 = 1.5484$ clears it with $0.0366$ bits of margin, so the collision explanation is quantitatively admissible.

The second half of Check C is recorded as a flag rather than a confirmation: the label-entropy drop is $4.6006-3.6073 = 0.9933$ bits while the information drop is $1.5484$ bits, and Theorem~\ref{thm:MIleH} forbids $\Delta I > \Delta H$ for a \emph{single} coarsening of a fixed joint weight. The two rows therefore cannot differ only by one merge of the joint label; at least one further difference (a second compression stage, a different marginalisation, or a different population restriction) is present. This is the intended use of the protocol: the ceiling confirms that collisions can explain the magnitude, while the sharp inequality localises a residual discrepancy for a targeted re-run. For calibration, the reported per-coordinate marginals are $1.0012$ bits each, summing to $2.0024$ against a joint value of $2.1314$; the excess of about $0.129$ bits is genuine synergy --- precisely the quantity a class merge destroys first.

\section{Algorithms}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Width audit for a multi-field key.} Input alphabet sizes $A_1,\dots,A_r$ and frames $M_1,\dots,M_r$ with $M_1=1$; output \textsc{valid} or the first violating index. $O(r)$ integer operations; correctness by Theorem~\ref{thm:iff} iterated.
\item \textbf{Exact collapse count.} Input $A,B,M$; output $A\cdot B$ if $M\ge B$ and $M(A-1)+B$ otherwise. $O(1)$; correctness by Theorem~\ref{thm:wide} and Corollary~\ref{cor:count}.
\item \textbf{Fiber profile and ceiling.} Input $A,B,M$ with $M \le B$; output the fiber sizes $\lvert\{a<A : 0 \le n-aM<B\}\rvert$ for each label $n$, the maximal fiber $k$, and the ceiling $\log_2 k$. $O(AB)$ by enumeration, or $O(1)$ per label from the closed form; correctness by Theorems~\ref{thm:Hceil} and~\ref{thm:MIceil}.
\item \textbf{Forensic reconciliation.} Input two rows $(\text{labels},H,I)$ from one population plus the encodings; output a verdict and a consistency report, by running the width audit on each encoding, applying Check D, then testing $\Delta I \le \log_2 k$ and $\Delta I \le \Delta H$.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Discussion}

Each ingredient is individually classical --- division with remainder, Gibbs' inequality, concavity of entropy, data processing. The contribution is their assembly into a decision procedure for a disputed measurement, with three sharpenings: an \emph{exact} (not asymptotic) collapse count with the image identified as an unbroken interval; a \emph{signed} verdict rule turning ``two runs disagree'' into an ordering; and a two-sided error bar whose upper end is attained, so the audit test is as tight as any universal test can be. The deficit calculus is of independent use as a self-contained treatment of entropy for \emph{unnormalised} finitely supported weights --- the natural setting for fiberwise arguments --- and it flags the absolute-continuity subtlety that the $0\log 0 = 0$ convention conceals.

Limitations. The ceiling $\log_2 k$ uses only the largest fiber, whereas the true loss is the mass-weighted average $\sum_u m_u \log_2\lvert f^{-1}(u)\rvert$. Theorem~\ref{thm:recon} compares two encodings of a \emph{fixed} population; if two runs also differ in filtering, binning or estimator, the verdict rule does not apply directly, though Theorem~\ref{thm:MIleH} will typically detect the difference. Everything is stated for finite alphabets and exact plug-in entropies; finite-sample bias is a separate source of discrepancy, biased \emph{upward} on small samples and hence distinguishable in principle from a collision artifact.

Practical recommendations. Use a tuple or factorised index rather than a chained integer where the language permits. Where chaining is unavoidable, compute frames from measured alphabet sizes rather than from decimal aesthetics ($10$, $100$, $10000$ are chosen for readability, and readability is not a correctness criterion), and assert the mixed-radix condition at pipeline entry. Log the distinct-label count next to every joint statistic: a discrepancy against the product of alphabet sizes is a zero-cost detector.

\section{Future directions}

\paragraph{Sharp collapse ceiling from the fiber profile.} The ceiling $\log_2 k$ uses only the largest fiber, whereas the true loss is the mass-weighted average $\sum_u m_u\log_2\lvert F_u\rvert$; for a chained frame the whole fiber profile is explicit, the fiber over $n$ having size $\lvert\{a<A : 0\le n-Ma<B\}\rvert$ when $M\le B$. Combining the per-fiber bound with the exact label set yields a closed formula for the worst-case entropy loss of an $(A,B,M)$ frame --- a lookup table to consult before running an experiment.

\paragraph{Reconstructibility.} The data-processing inequality has a computable defect (the fiber deficits), so a coarsened reading plus the fiber profile brackets the true reading from both sides; for a $k$-bounded distortion the true value is recoverable to within $\log_2 k$. This would let a retracted number be repaired rather than discarded, at the cost of a widened error bar.

\paragraph{Multi-dial chaining and a width calculus.} Chaining $r$ dials is injective precisely under the mixed-radix condition $M_i \ge A_{i-1}M_{i-1}$ (with $M_1=1$), so width checking becomes a small calculus on frame vectors, with a canonical minimal-frame normal form and a notion of slack measuring how much headroom a key has before a new category breaks it.

\paragraph{Estimator-level integration.} Combining the collapse ceiling with finite-sample bias bounds for plug-in entropy estimators would give a single interval within which two readings of one population must lie if they differ only by encoding and sampling.

\section{Conclusion}

A chained integer label $\pi_M(a,b)=aM+b$ is faithful if and only if the frame dominates the inner alphabet, $B\le M$; otherwise it collides on every population with at least two outer codes and reports exactly $M(A-1)+B$ classes in place of $A\cdot B$ --- on a $4\times9$ population with $M=3$, eighteen in place of thirty-six. Merging classes destroys entropy, strictly whenever two merged classes are populated, and can only decrease measured mutual information, while an injective re-encoding changes nothing at all. Hence a width-valid reading dominates every other reading of the same population, and the damage a merge can do is bounded by $\log_2 k$, attained. from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random
from itertools import product
from typing import Callable, Dict, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

Pair = Tuple[int, int]

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Chained labels and the width criterion
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------


def chain(frame: int, outer: int, inner: int) -> int:
    """The chained integer label  pi_M(a, b) = a * M + b."""
    return outer * frame + inner


def population(a_size: int, b_size: int) -> List[Pair]:
    """All genuine code pairs {0..A-1} x {0..B-1}."""
    return [(a, b) for a in range(a_size) for b in range(b_size)]


def width_ok(b_size: int, frame: int) -> bool:
    """The audit check: the frame must dominate the inner alphabet."""
    return b_size <= frame


def has_collision(a_size: int, b_size: int, frame: int) -> bool:
    """Brute-force search for two distinct pairs sharing a chained label."""
    seen: Dict[int, Pair] = {}
    for pair in population(a_size, b_size):
        label = chain(frame, *pair)
        if label in seen and seen[label] != pair:
            return True
        seen[label] = pair
    return False


def distinct_labels(a_size: int, b_size: int, frame: int) -> int:
    """Number of distinct chained labels actually produced."""
    return len({chain(frame, a, b) for a, b in population(a_size, b_size)})


def predicted_labels(a_size: int, b_size: int, frame: int) -> int:
    """Closed form: A*B if the frame is wide, else M*(A-1)+B."""
    if frame >= b_size:

    return frame * (a_size - 1) + b_size


def fiber_profile(a_size: int, b_size: int, frame: int) -> Dict[int, List[Pair]]:
    """Map each produced label to the list of genuine pairs merged into it."""
    fibers: Dict[int, List[Pair]] = {}
    for pair in population(a_size, b_size):

    return fibers

# 2. Entropy in bits, and the deficit of a merged block
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------


def eta(t: float) -> float:
    """Pointwise Shannon term -t*log2(t), with the convention eta(0) = 0."""
    return 0.0 if t <= 0.0 else -t * math.log2(t)


def entropy(weights: Iterable[float]) -> float:
    """Shannon entropy (bits) of a nonnegative, not necessarily normalised weight."""
    return sum(eta(w) for w in weights)


def deficit(weights: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Entropy destroyed by collapsing a block into one atom of the total mass."""
    return entropy(weights) - eta(sum(weights))


def deficit_closed_form(weights: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """The closed form  sum_i w_i * (log2 S - log2 w_i),  S = sum_i w_i."""
    total = sum(weights)
    if total <= 0.0:
        return 0.0
    return sum(w * (math.log2(total) - math.log2(w)) for w in weights if w > 0.0)


def deficit_ceiling(weights: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """The maximum-entropy bound  (block mass) * log2(block size)."""
    n = len(weights)
    return sum(weights) * math.log2(n) if n > 0 else 0.0

Joint = Dict[Tuple[Pair, int], float]


def marginal_first(joint: Joint) -> Dict[Pair, float]:
    out: Dict[Pair, float] = {}
    for (x, _y), w in joint.items():
        out[x] = out.get(x, 0.0) + w
    return out


def marginal_second(joint: Joint) -> Dict[int, float]:
    out: Dict[int, float] = {}
    for (_x, y), w in joint.items():
        out[y] = out.get(y, 0.0) + w
    return out


def mutual_information(joint: Joint) -> float:
    """I(p) = H(first marginal) + H(second marginal) - H(joint), in bits."""
    return (
        entropy(marginal_first(joint).values())
        + entropy(marginal_second(joint).values())
        - entropy(joint.values())
    )


def push_first(joint: Joint, label: Callable[[Pair], int]) -> Dict[Tuple[int, int], float]:
    """Relabel the first coordinate, summing the weights of merged classes."""
    out: Dict[Tuple[int, int], float] = {}
    for (x, y), w in joint.items():
        key = (label(x), y)
        out[key] = out.get(key, 0.0) + w
    return out


def mutual_information_generic(joint: Dict[Tuple[object, object], float]) -> float:
    first: Dict[object, float] = {}
    second: Dict[object, float] = {}
    for (x, y), w in joint.items():
        first[x] = first.get(x, 0.0) + w
        second[y] = second.get(y, 0.0) + w
    return entropy(first.values()) + entropy(second.values()) - entropy(joint.values())


def push_entropy(joint: Dict[Tuple[object, object], float]) -> float:
    """Entropy of the (relabelled) first marginal -- the 'label entropy' column."""
    first: Dict[object, float] = {}
    for (x, _y), w in joint.items():

    return entropy(first.values())

    for a, b in population(a_size, b_size):

    return sum(eta(w) for w in weights)


def deficit(weights: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Entropy destroyed by collapsing a block into one atom of the total mass."""
    return entropy(weights) - eta(sum(weights))


def deficit_closed_form(weights: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """The closed form  sum_i w_i * (log2 S - log2 w_i),  S = sum_i w_i."""
    total = sum(weights)
    if total <= 0.0:
        return 0.0
    return sum(w * (math.log2(total) - math.log2(w)) for w in weights if w > 0.0)


def deficit_ceiling(weights: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """The maximum-entropy bound  (block mass) * log2(block size)."""
    n = len(weights)
    return sum(weights) * math.log2(n) if n > 0 else 0.0


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Joint weights, pushforwards, mutual information
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

Joint = Dict[Tuple[Pair, int], float]


def marginal_first(joint: Joint) -> Dict[Pair, float]:
    out: Dict[Pair, float] = {}
    for (x, _y), w in joint.items():
        out[x] = out.get(x, 0.0) + w
    return out


def marginal_second(joint: Joint) -> Dict[int, float]:
    out: Dict[int, float] = {}
    for (_x, y), w in joint.items():
        out[y] = out.get(y, 0.0) + w
    return out


def mutual_information(joint: Joint) -> float:
    """I(p) = H(first marginal) + H(second marginal) - H(joint), in bits."""
    return (
        entropy(marginal_first(joint).values())
        + entropy(marginal_second(joint).values())
        - entropy(joint.values())
    )


def push_first(joint: Joint, label: Callable[[Pair], int]) -> Dict[Tuple[int, int], float]:
    """Relabel the first coordinate, summing the weights of merged classes."""
    out: Dict[Tuple[int, int], float] = {}
    for (x, y), w in joint.items():
        key = (label(x), y)
        out[key] = out.get(key, 0.0) + w
    return out


def mutual_information_generic(joint: Dict[Tuple[object, object], float]) -> float:
    first: Dict[object, float] = {}
    second: Dict[object, float] = {}
    for (x, y), w in joint.items():
        first[x] = first.get(x, 0.0) + w
        second[y] = second.get(y, 0.0) + w
    return entropy(first.values()) + entropy(second.values()) - entropy(joint.values())


def push_entropy(joint: Dict[Tuple[object, object], float]) -> float:
    """Entropy of the (relabelled) first marginal -- the 'label entropy' column."""
    first: Dict[object, float] = {}
    for (x, _y), w in joint.items():
        first[x] = first.get(x, 0.0) + w
    return entropy(first.values())

def random_joint(a_size: int, b_size: int, y_size: int, seed: int = 20260822) -> Joint:
    """A random joint probability weight on (code pairs) x (outcomes)."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    raw = {
        ((a, b), y): rng.random() ** 2
        for a, b in population(a_size, b_size)
        for y in range(y_size)
    }
    total = sum(raw.values())
    return {k: v / total for k, v in raw.items()}


def structured_joint(a_size: int, b_size: int, y_size: int, seed: int = 7,
                     signal: float = 0.85) -> Joint:
    """A joint weight with a genuine channel: the outcome depends on the pair."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    raw: Joint = {}
    for a, b in population(a_size, b_size):
        preferred = (a + b) % y_size
        for y in range(y_size):
            base = signal if y == preferred else (1.0 - signal) / max(y_size - 1, 1)
            raw[((a, b), y)] = base * (0.5 + rng.random())
    total = sum(raw.values())
    return {k: v / total for k, v in raw.items()}

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import List, Optional, Sequence


@dataclass
class WidthAuditReport:
    """Outcome of a width audit on a chained key."""
    valid: bool
    first_violation: Optional[int]        # index i with M[i+1] < A[i]*M[i]
    required_frames: List[int]            # the minimal admissible frame vector
    genuine_classes: int                  # product of the alphabet sizes
    reported_classes: Optional[int]       # exact class count when r == 2


def minimal_frames(alphabets: Sequence[int]) -> List[int]:
    """Minimal mixed-radix frame vector: M[0] = 1, M[i+1] = A[i] * M[i]."""
    frames = [1]
    for size in alphabets[:-1]:
        frames.append(frames[-1] * size)
    return frames


def two_dial_class_count(a_size: int, b_size: int, frame: int) -> int:
    """Exact number of labels produced by pi_M(a,b) = a*M + b on A x B."""
    if frame >= b_size:
        return a_size * b_size
    return frame * (a_size - 1) + b_size


def width_audit(alphabets: Sequence[int], frames: Sequence[int]) -> WidthAuditReport:
    """Audit a chained key sum_i a_i * M_i against its alphabet sizes.

    The key is injective if and only if M[0] == 1 and M[i+1] >= A[i]*M[i]
    for every i; this is an equivalence, not a sufficient condition.

    Complexity: O(r) integer operations for r dials.
    """
    if len(alphabets) != len(frames):
        raise ValueError("alphabets and frames must have equal length")
    genuine = 1
    for size in alphabets:
        genuine *= size

    violation: Optional[int] = None
    if frames and frames[0] != 1:
        violation = 0
    else:
        for i in range(len(frames) - 1):
            if frames[i + 1] < alphabets[i] * frames[i]:
                violation = i
                break

    reported = None
    if len(alphabets) == 2:
        # canonical two-dial form pi(a,b) = a*M + b, i.e. frames == (1, M)
        reported = two_dial_class_count(alphabets[1], alphabets[0], frames[1])

    return WidthAuditReport(
        valid=violation is None,
        first_violation=violation,
        required_frames=minimal_frames(alphabets),
        genuine_classes=genuine,
        reported_classes=reported,
    )

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple


def fiber_size(label: int, a_size: int, b_size: int, frame: int) -> int:
    """|{a < A : 0 <= label - a*M < B}| -- the number of pairs merged into `label`.

    Closed form, O(1): the admissible outer codes form the integer interval
    [ceil((label - B + 1)/M), floor(label/M)] intersected with [0, A-1].
    """
    if frame <= 0:
        return a_size if 0 <= label < b_size else 0
    lo = max(0, -((b_size - 1 - label) // frame))       # ceil((label-B+1)/M)
    hi = min(a_size - 1, label // frame)
    return max(0, hi - lo + 1)


def fiber_profile(a_size: int, b_size: int, frame: int) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Label -> fiber size, for every label the frame can produce.

    Complexity: O(#labels) with the O(1) closed form above, i.e. O(M*A + B)
    for a narrow frame, versus O(A*B) for naive enumeration.
    """
    n_labels = a_size * b_size if frame >= b_size else frame * (a_size - 1) + b_size
    span = range(n_labels) if frame < b_size else sorted(
        {a * frame + b for a in range(a_size) for b in range(b_size)}
    )
    return {n: fiber_size(n, a_size, b_size, frame) for n in span}


def collapse_ceiling(a_size: int, b_size: int, frame: int) -> Tuple[int, float]:
    """Maximal fiber size k and the ceiling log2(k) on the destroyable bits.

    A k-bounded label merge destroys at most log2(k) bits of label entropy and
    at most log2(k) bits of mutual information, and the bound is attained by a
    uniform k-atom fiber, so no smaller universal ceiling exists.
    """
    profile = fiber_profile(a_size, b_size, frame)
    k = max(profile.values()) if profile else 1
    return k, math.log2(max(k, 1))


def uniform_label_entropy(a_size: int, b_size: int, frame: int) -> float:
    """Label entropy (bits) of the uniform population under the given frame."""
    total = a_size * b_size
    profile = fiber_profile(a_size, b_size, frame)
    return -sum(
        (size / total) * math.log2(size / total)
        for size in profile.values()
        if size > 0
    )


def exact_uniform_loss(a_size: int, b_size: int, frame: int) -> float:
    """Entropy destroyed on the uniform population: the mass-weighted average

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import List, Optional


@dataclass
class Reading:
    """One reported row: an encoding frame plus the statistics computed under it."""
    name: str
    frame: int
    labels: int
    label_entropy: float      # H(labels), bits
    mutual_information: float  # I(joint), bits


@dataclass
class Verdict:
    admissible: Optional[str]     # name of the reading that must be believed
    artifact: Optional[str]       # name of the reading that must be an artifact
    ceiling_bits: float           # log2 k for the suspect encoding
    information_drop: float
    entropy_drop: float
    ceiling_test: bool            # dI <= log2 k
    sharp_test: bool              # dI <= dH
    notes: List[str]


def fiber_size(label: int, a_size: int, b_size: int, frame: int) -> int:
    lo = max(0, -((b_size - 1 - label) // frame))
    hi = min(a_size - 1, label // frame)
    return max(0, hi - lo + 1)


def max_fiber(a_size: int, b_size: int, frame: int) -> int:
    if frame >= b_size:
        return 1
    n_labels = frame * (a_size - 1) + b_size
    return max(fiber_size(n, a_size, b_size, frame) for n in range(n_labels))


def reconcile(a_size: int, b_size: int, wide: Reading, suspect: Reading) -> Verdict:
    """Adjudicate two readings of the same population.

    Check D (direction): a width-valid encoding is injective, so it reports the
    true value, and every other encoding reports at most that value.  Hence the
    larger reading is admissible and the smaller is the artifact.

    Check C (ceiling): with k the maximal fiber of the suspect encoding, the
    information drop must satisfy dI <= log2 k, and additionally dI <= dH where
    dH is the drop in label entropy.  A violation of either proves the two
    pipelines differ in more than their label encoding.

    Complexity: O(#labels) for the fiber scan, O(1) for the tests.
    """
    notes: List[str] = []
    k = max_fiber(a_size, b_size, suspect.frame)
    ceiling = math.log2(max(k, 1))
    d_i = wide.mutual_information - suspect.mutual_information
    d_h = wide.label_entropy - suspect.label_entropy

    if b_size <= wide.frame:
        admissible, artifact = wide.name, suspect.name
        notes.append(
            f"'{wide.name}' is width-valid ({b_size} <= {wide.frame}) and therefore "
            f"injective; '{suspect.name}' uses frame {suspect.frame} < {b_size} and "
            f"must collide, so it can only under-report.")
    else:
        admissible = artifact = None
        notes.append("Neither encoding is width-valid: no verdict is available.")

    predicted = suspect.frame * (a_size - 1) + b_size if suspect.frame < b_size \
        else a_size * b_size
    notes.append(
        f"predicted class count under the suspect frame: {predicted} "
        f"(reported {suspect.labels}) against {a_size * b_size} genuine pairs.")

    ceiling_test = d_i <= ceiling + 1e-12
    sharp_test = d_i <= d_h + 1e-12
    if not ceiling_test:
        notes.append(
            f"CEILING VIOLATED: a {k}-bounded merge can destroy at most "
            f"{ceiling:.4f} bits, but {d_i:.4f} bits are missing; the encoding "
            f"alone cannot explain the gap.")
    if not sharp_test:
        notes.append(
            f"SHARP TEST VIOLATED: information lost ({d_i:.4f} bits) exceeds label "
            f"entropy lost ({d_h:.4f} bits), which one coarsening of a fixed joint "
            f"weight cannot do; the pipelines differ in more than the frame.")
    if ceiling_test and sharp_test:
        notes.append("Both consistency tests pass: a pure collision artifact "
                     "fully accounts for the discrepancy.")

    return Verdict(admissible, artifact, ceiling, d_i, d_h,
                   ceiling_test, sharp_test, notes)

*A guided tour of chained integer labels: why they collide, exactly how many classes they destroy, which of two disagreeing measurements must be believed, and how large a discrepancy a collision is allowed to explain.*

---

## 1. The setting: two codes, one integer

Almost every data pipeline eventually needs to treat a *pair* of categorical variables as a single categorical variable. Suppose each observation carries an outer code $a \in \{0,\dots,A-1\}$ and an inner code $b \in \{0,\dots,B-1\}$. The universal idiom is to pick a **frame** $M$ and build the *chained label*

$$\pi_M(a,b) \;=\; a\cdot M + b .$$

With $M = 10000$, the pair $(3,7)$ becomes $30007$: you can literally read the two components off the digits. It is a decimal filing system — the outer code in the high digits, the inner code in the low digits.

It works perfectly, right up until the low digits are too narrow to hold the inner code. If $b$ can reach $8$ but you chose $M = 3$, then

$$\pi_3(0,3) = 3 = \pi_3(1,0),$$

and two genuinely different observations have been filed in the same drawer. No error, no warning; every downstream statistic is now computed on a *coarsening* of your data.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

2. At $M < B$ the class labels produced form an *unbroken run* $0,1,2,\dots$ with no gaps — that is not an accident, it is a theorem.
3. The "bits actually destroyed" bar never fills past the ceiling $\log_2 k$, and it touches the ceiling only when the fibers are uniform.

## 2. The width criterion — and why it is an equivalence, not a rule of thumb

**Theorem (Width Criterion).** *Let $A \ge 2$. The chaining $\pi_M$ is injective on $\{0,\dots,A-1\}\times\{0,\dots,B-1\}$ **if and only if** $B \le M$.*

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal the proof (it is two lines in each direction)</summary>

**Sufficiency.** If $b < M$ then $M > 0$ and division with remainder decodes the label:
$$\left\lfloor \frac{aM+b}{M}\right\rfloor = a, \qquad (aM+b) \bmod M = b .$$
So the label determines the pair. Division with remainder *is* the decoder.

**Necessity.** If $M < B$ then $(0,M)$ and $(1,0)$ are both admissible pairs, they are different, and
$$\pi_M(0,M) = M = \pi_M(1,0).$$
So the failure is structural: there is no data set on which a too-narrow frame is safe.

</details>

This equivalence is why the one-line check `inner_alphabet_size <= frame` is worth so much: it is neither conservative nor optimistic. A pipeline that passes it *cannot* have this bug; one that fails it *does* have it. For a key with $r$ fields, $\sum_i a_i M_i$ with $M_1 = 1$, the criterion iterates into the familiar mixed-radix condition $M_{i+1} \ge A_i M_i$.

Here is the check as running code, together with the closed-form prediction of how many classes a broken key will report.

{{algorithm:0}}

## 3. Exactly how many drawers are left?

Knowing that a merge happened is not enough; an auditor wants a number. There is an exact one.

**Theorem (Exact Collapse Count).** *If $M \le B$ and $A \ge 1$, the set of labels produced is precisely the interval $\{0,1,\dots,M(A-1)+B-1\}$. Hence the number of distinct classes reported is exactly*
$$M(A-1) + B,$$
*against $A\cdot B$ genuine pairs — strictly fewer whenever $M < B$ and $A \ge 2$.*

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal the shingle argument</summary>

Outer code $a$ contributes the *strip* of labels $[aM,\; aM+B)$. Consecutive strips start $M$ apart but are $B$ long. When $M \le B$ they overlap like roof shingles, so their union has no gaps and runs from $0$ to the top of the last strip, namely $M(A-1)+B$.

Conversely every $n$ below that bound is hit: if $n < M(A-1)$ take $a = \lfloor n/M\rfloor$, $b = n \bmod M$ (legal because $b < M \le B$); otherwise take $a = A-1$ and $b = n - M(A-1)$, which lies in $[0,B)$ exactly because of the two bounds on $n$.

Strictness: $M \le B-1$ gives $M(A-1)+B \le (B-1)(A-1)+B = AB-(A-1) < AB$.

</details>

Substituting the audited population $A = 4$, $B = 9$ and the narrow frame $M = 3$:

$$3\cdot(4-1) + 9 \;=\; 18 \qquad\text{against}\qquad 4\cdot 9 = 36 .$$

Exactly half the classes, gone. The picture below draws the shingles for several frames, so you can see the overlaps that are doing the damage.

## 4. From lost drawers to lost bits

Counting classes is combinatorics; the scientific claims were about *information*. So we need to know precisely what merging does to entropy.

Write $\eta(t) = -t\log_2 t$ (with $\eta(0)=0$) and $H_s(w) = \sum_{i\in s}\eta(w_i)$ for a nonnegative, not necessarily normalised, weight. The right object is the **deficit** of a block: the entropy destroyed by collapsing all of $s$ into one atom carrying the total mass $S = \sum_i w_i$,

$$D_s(w) \;=\; H_s(w) - \eta(S) \;=\; \sum_{i\in s} w_i\bigl(\log_2 S - \log_2 w_i\bigr).$$

Three facts follow, and they are the whole engine of what comes later.

| statement | content |
|---|---|
| $D_s(w) \ge 0$ | **merging always loses** — each term is $w_i\log_2(S/w_i)\ge 0$ |
| $D_s(w) > 0$ if two atoms are positive | **merging strictly loses** |
| $D_s(w) \le S\log_2 \lvert s\rvert$, with equality for uniform $w$ | **the loss is capped, and the cap is attained** |

<details>
<summary>A trap worth knowing: Gibbs' inequality can go negative</summary>

The upper bound above is Gibbs' inequality in disguise — compare $w$ against the uniform weight of the same total mass and the relative entropy between them, being nonnegative, is exactly the slack.

But relative entropy is **not** unconditionally nonnegative under the convenient convention $0\log 0 = 0$. Take true weights $(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$ and comparison weights $(1,0)$: same total mass, yet
$$\tfrac12(\log_2\tfrac12 - \log_2 1) + \tfrac12(\log_2\tfrac12 - \log_2 0) \;=\; -\tfrac12 - \tfrac12 \;=\; -1 \;<\; 0 .$$
The missing hypothesis is *absolute continuity*: the comparison weights must not vanish where the real ones do not. Under the $\log 0 = 0$ convention an infinite penalty silently becomes a zero penalty. Every use of Gibbs here carries an explicit absolute-continuity argument. See also the classical background on [Gibbs' inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibbs%27_inequality) and [entropy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entropy_(information_theory)).

</details>

There is one more ingredient, the least obvious and the most powerful: **superadditivity of the deficit**. If a nonnegative weight $w$ is split into a family of pieces $v^{(y)}$ with $\sum_y v^{(y)} = w$, then

$$\sum_y D_s\bigl(v^{(y)}\bigr) \;\le\; D_s(w).$$

This is the concavity of entropy, rewritten so that it can be applied one fiber at a time. It is what lets a statement about blocks become a statement about channels.

---

## 5. The two theorems that settle a dispute

Now consider a joint weight $p$ on pairs $(x,y)$, where $x$ is the thing being labelled and $y$ is whatever the channel is measured against, with mutual information $I(p) = H(p_1) + H(p_2) - H(p)$. Relabel the first coordinate by $f$, summing the weights of merged classes.

**Theorem (Encoding Invariance).** *If $f$ is injective then $I(f_\sharp p) = I(p)$.*

Relabelling is renaming, not analysis. Two clean implementations that both satisfy the width criterion compute the same functional of the same data, so they must agree **exactly** — and *approximate* agreement between two allegedly exact pipelines is itself an anomaly worth chasing.

**Theorem (Signed Data Processing).** *For any $f$ whatsoever and any nonnegative $p$, $I(f_\sharp p) \le I(p)$.*

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal the proof sketch</summary>

The second marginal is untouched by a relabelling of the first coordinate, so
$$I(p) - I(f_\sharp p) \;=\; \underbrace{\bigl[H(p_1) - H(f_*p_1)\bigr]}_{\text{marginal loss}} - \underbrace{\bigl[H(p) - H(f_\sharp p)\bigr]}_{\text{joint loss}} .$$
Each loss is a sum of fiber deficits: the marginal loss is $\sum_u D_{f^{-1}(u)}(p_1)$, the joint loss is $\sum_u \sum_y D_{f^{-1}(u)}(p(\cdot,y))$. Since $p_1 = \sum_y p(\cdot,y)$, superadditivity applied on each fiber gives joint loss $\le$ marginal loss, so the difference is nonnegative.

</details>

Put together:

> **The Reconciliation.** On one and the same population, a width-valid encoding reports the true value and *every* other encoding reports at most that value.

Collision artifacts are **signed**: they deflate a measurement, never inflate it. So when two runs on an identical population disagree and one is width-valid, the larger number is the admissible one — and the corrupted analysis is the one that *looks* cautious, which is precisely why nobody's alarm goes off.

The demo below verifies all of this numerically on a synthetic channel: identical readings for every width-valid frame, monotone decreasing readings as the frame narrows, and every drop within its ceiling.

## 6. An error bar for the error

A one-sided law fixes the direction of a discrepancy but not its size — and without a size bound, "collisions did it" is unfalsifiable. So the converse matters just as much.

**Theorem (Collapse Ceiling).** *If no class collects more than $k$ originals, then the merge destroys at most $\log_2 k$ bits of label entropy and at most $\log_2 k$ bits of mutual information — whatever the size of the population or the strength of the channel. The bound is attained by a uniform fiber, so no smaller universal ceiling exists.*

Two corollaries do most of the day-to-day work:

* **A two-to-one merge costs at most one bit.** Always.
* **Contrapositive:** a drop of more than one bit *proves* that some class swallowed at least **three** originals. If the encoding has no such triple merge, the two pipelines differ in something other than their labels.

And the sharpest test of all, which needs only two columns of a printed results table:

$$\Delta I \;\le\; \Delta H : \qquad \text{information lost never exceeds label entropy lost.}$$

The visualization below plots, for a fixed population, the universal ceiling $\log_2 k$ against the loss that actually occurs — the shaded band is the slack an audit gives up by looking only at the worst fiber, and closing that band is an open direction.

{{visualization:1}}

The fiber profile behind both curves is itself an explicit arithmetic object: under a narrow frame the class $n$ swallows exactly $\lvert\{a < A: 0 \le n - aM < B\}\rvert$ pairs, computable in $O(1)$.

{{algorithm:1}}

| original | $a\cdot 10000+b$ | $36$ | $4.6006$ | $2.1314$ |
| independent clean re-implementation | width-valid | $36$ | $4.6006$ | $2.1314$ |
| rebuild | narrow nested frame | $18$ | $3.6073$ | $0.5830$ |

**Check W.** The rebuild's frame is narrower than the alphabet below it, so it *must* collide, and $36 \to 18$ is exactly the predicted $M(A-1)+B$ with $(A,B,M) = (4,9,3)$.

**Check C.** The largest narrow-frame fiber is $3$, giving a ceiling of $\log_2 3 \approx 1.5850$ bits. The observed gap $2.1314 - 0.5830 = 1.5484$ clears it with $0.0366$ bits to spare: the collision story is quantitatively admissible.
